## Abstract

Previous research suggests an association between posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and metabolic syndrome (MetS) but has not disentangled effects of trauma exposure, PTSD, and psychological resilience following trauma. This study investigated risk of MetS by psychological resilience following trauma exposure.

Data are from 42,425 women in the Nurses’ Health Study II who completed a survey in 2008 evaluating PTSD symptoms, psychological distress, facets of positive psychological well-being (PWB), and a broad range of covariates. Psychological resilience to trauma was characterized as: resilient (no PTSD and high positive PWB), coping without thriving (no PTSD and low positive PWB), and PTSD, with a no trauma control group. Probable MetS was derived using data on weight, height, diagnosed hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes, and medication use from biennial surveys between 1989–2019. Time to probable MetS was approximated as the return date of the first questionnaire at which 3+ probable MetS criteria were met.

Proportional hazards models adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics indicated that, relative to women with no trauma, women categorized as having PTSD (aHR = 1.34 [1.05, 1.71]) or as coping without thriving (aHR = 1.29 [1.03, 1.62]) experienced a greater hazard of developing MetS, whereas resilient women experienced a similar hazard of developing MetS (aHR = 1.06 [0.84, 1.34]). Results remained similar after adjusting for health behaviors and antidepressant use.

Future research on trauma and MetS should consider varied trauma responses and assess if interventions that not only reduce psychological distress but also promote PWB could mitigate MetS risk.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in women globally, accounting for 1 in 3 deaths.1 Although extensive awareness and prevention efforts have contributed to a general decline in the age-standardized prevalence of CVD since 1990, the rate of improvement has slowed substantially since 2010.1,2 The reasons underpinning this deceleration remain unknown. However, existing literature has largely attributed it to the concomitant increase in the prevalence of CVD risk factors,2–4 namely obesity,4 diabetes and insulin resistance,5 dyslipidemia,6 and hypertension.7,8 The co-occurrence of three or more of these risk factors plus hypertriglyceridemia is associated with 1.32–2.72 times the risk of CVD relative to individuals with fewer than three risk factors.9–11 This clustering of risk factors, designated as metabolic syndrome (MetS), accounts for an estimated 27–67% of CVD deaths in women.12–14 Prevalence of MetS in the United States (US) has increased substantially since 1988 across all demographic groups, affecting 37%-46% of US adults currently.15–19 In addition to conventional risk factors like health behaviors, some work suggests psychological factors may also affect risk of developing MetS and provide novel targets for intervention. Identification and mitigation of psychological risk factors for MetS offers a potential avenue through which to minimize CVD risk and premature mortality in women.12,20

Accumulating evidence suggests posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may increase risk for MetS.21–23 A 2015 meta-analysis of nine studies found individuals with PTSD had an 82% greater risk of MetS relative to the general population.20 However, only one of the studies was prospective, and it was conducted among predominantly male veterans.24 Although women experience a greater burden of PTSD25 and are at greater risk for downstream consequences of MetS than men,12,14,26 most research on PTSD and MetS has been conducted in male veterans.20,21,27,28 Moreover, studies investigating the association in civilian populations have primarily used cross-sectional data.23,29–31 To our knowledge, only one prospective study has investigated the association between PTSD and MetS among civilians and findings were suggestive; using claims data from the Taiwanese National Health Insurance program, Lin and colleagues32 found that women with versus without a PTSD diagnosis had 3.62 times the hazard of incident MetS, but effects of trauma exposure alone or other forms of distress were not considered.

Relationships between MetS and psychological resilience to trauma have received little attention. Most individuals exposed to trauma will not develop PTSD,33–35 although some may develop other psychological disorders (e.g. depression), subclinical levels of distress, or experience low levels of positive psychological well-being (e.g. hope, meaning in life). Other individuals will exhibit high levels of resilience, or favorable psychological health even in the face of trauma exposure.36,37 This type of psychological resilience to trauma has been defined as the ability to maintain or regain mental health in the face of adversity and, by doing so, avoid or minimize the negative psychological and physiological consequences of traumatic experiences.38,39

Although resilience has often been conceptualized as an individual capacity or a trait,40,41 more recently, scholars have adopted an outcome-based conceptualization of resilience – that is, rather than characterizing how individuals perceive they might respond to trauma, individuals are characterized as resilient or not according to their response to actual trauma. Specifically, resilience is defined as demonstrating low levels of psychological distress while maintaining positive psychological well-being (e.g. optimism, positive affect/happiness) following exposure to trauma.38,42 Evidence suggests that most individuals do not go on to experience chronically high levels of psychological distress in following trauma exposure,43 but the extent to which individuals who experience trauma, even absent severe distress, can maintain healthy psychological functioning varies. In recent work, psychological resilience to trauma is defined as a state that exceeds the mere absence of psychopathological conditions following trauma exposure; it further involves the experience of facets of positive psychological well-being such as optimism and life satisfaction.38,44 Notably, prior work has also found that multiple facets of positive psychological well-being are related to a more favorable metabolic profile.45

Throughout this article, we use the terms psychological health, positive psychological well-being, and psychological resilience to refer to three closely related but distinct constructs. Psychological health encompasses both positive (e.g., optimism, happiness) and negative (e.g., symptoms of psychopathology) facets of psychological functioning, whereas positive psychological well-being refers exclusively to the favorable aspects of psychological health. Psychological resilience refers to psychological health specifically in the context of one’s trauma burden. For example, individuals may have high psychological resilience if they exhibit relatively favorable psychological health in the context of numerous traumatic events, even if their psychological health is less favorable than that which is observed among individuals who have no trauma exposure.

Limited research has explicitly examined specifically whether variations in psychological resilience to trauma are related to risk of developing MetS, although prior work has identified aspects of psychological health (or lack thereof) without accounting for trauma history as protective or risk factors for cardiometabolic outcomes.46–49 Recent studies have suggested that individuals who maintain psychological health after exposure to trauma may have lower risk of developing cardiometabolic disease,50 COVID-19 infection,51 and be less likely to engage in adverse health behaviors52 relative to those who experience psychological distress. To the best of our knowledge, no research has investigated which facets of positive psychological well-being may be most relevant to cardiometabolic risk following trauma exposure. However, literature on positive psychological well-being and cardiometabolic disease more broadly has highlighted positive affect,53 optimism,54 purpose and meaning,55,56 and life satisfaction57 as particularly relevant to cardiovascular and metabolic health. Together, these results suggest psychological resilience to trauma may promote physical health or mitigate potential harmful effects of trauma on downstream physical health outcomes.

## Current Study

The present study leverages data from the Nurses’ Health Study II (NHS2), a large and well-characterized longitudinal cohort of professional women, to compare associations between three distinct responses to trauma with no trauma exposure in relation to risk of developing MetS among women. Using information on trauma burden, levels of distress, and facets of positive psychological well-being, we characterized women with trauma exposure as exhibiting resilience (i.e., favorable psychological health relative to one’s trauma burden), coping without thriving (i.e., unfavorable psychological health relative to one’s trauma burden in the absence of criteria for PTSD), and probable PTSD. In doing so, we aimed to investigate if the rate of developing MetS following trauma exposure varies with psychological resilience to trauma and theoretically derived forms of psychological functioning, namely PTSD.

Considering women who were not trauma exposed as the reference group, we hypothesized that women with PTSD would have the highest risk of developing MetS over the 10 years of follow-up, but that women characterized as coping without thriving (trauma-exposed with few or no PTSD symptoms but low resilience) would also have elevated risk. This hypothesis was motivated by extant evidence suggesting PTSD is associated with a greater risk of metabolic syndrome relative to general population controls (risk ratio [95% CI] = 1.82 [1.72, 1.92])20 than depression (odds ratio (OR) = 1.48 [1.33, 1.64])48 or general stress (OR = 1.45 [1.21, 1.74]).58 Since the odds ratio overestimates the risk ratio when the outcome is common,59 the corresponding estimated risk ratios for depression and general stress are necessarily lower than the estimate for PTSD. In addition, we hypothesized that women characterized as being resilient would exhibit a risk of MetS similar to that of women with no trauma exposure. We also characterized women according to a continuous measure of resilience by leveraging information on psychological health and cumulative trauma burden, and evaluated the extent to which variation across the continuum of psychological resilience was associated with the rate of developing MetS. We considered a broad array of potential confounders of the association between psychological resilience and other responses to trauma, based on prior literature suggesting these factors are relevant.50,51 Furthermore, to evaluate if identified associations may be driven by specific MetS criteria, we investigated the associations of resilience and other responses to trauma with each criterion separately, as well as the association with a count score of number of MetS criteria that were met. By providing insight into the association between a range of responses to trauma exposure and MetS, we aimed to identify trauma-exposed individuals at greatest risk of MetS and inform strategies for the improvement of health outcomes among trauma-exposed populations.38,39

## Methods

### Study Sample

The NHS2 is a prospective cohort study of 116,429 female registered nurses from 14 states across the US. Since enrollment at ages 25–42 years in 1989, cohort members have completed biennial questionnaires about their health and health behaviors. Follow-up has consistently been high (≥ 85%) and is ongoing. The design and procedures of the NHS2 are detailed elsewhere.60 In addition to the biennial questionnaires, in 2008 cohort members were invited to complete a supplemental questionnaire assessing lifetime trauma exposure and PTSD (N = 54,701; response rate = 89.9%).61 The study protocol was approved by the institutional review boards of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

The sample for this study included 42,425 women who responded to the 2008 PTSD questionnaire and also to the 2009 biennial questionnaire, had never met criteria for probable MetS as of 2009 (see Probable Metabolic Syndrome below), and responded to at least one biennial questionnaire after 2009. Participants’ responses to the 2009 questionnaire were necessary to exclude individuals with prevalent MetS. We evaluated associations with MetS as well as with each MetS component separately, and samples for analyses with individual components were defined similarly. To this end, we excluded women with the condition at the time trauma and related psychological responses were assessed, resulting in slightly different sample sizes depending on the component under consideration as follows: hypertension (N = 29,706), hyperlipidemia (N = 24,433), diabetes (N = 47,790), and overweight/obesity (N = 28,145). Individuals missing sufficient information to calculate psychological responses to trauma were excluded from all analyses (N = 1,588). Additional information on sample derivation is available in Figure S1 (Supplemental Digital Content 1). Sociodemographic characteristics of the full NHS2 cohort, respondents to the 2008 PTSD questionnaire, and primary analytic sample were broadly similar (see Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content 1). Notably, relative to the whole cohort, individuals in the primary analytic sample were slightly less likely to be current smokers at baseline (10.6% versus 13.5%), had somewhat lower BMI (mean [standard deviation] = 22.8 [5.1] versus 24.1 [3.8]), and were slightly less likely to endorse clinician-diagnosed depression or regular use of antidepressant medication between 1989 and 2009 (36% versus 39.7%).

### Trauma and Response to Trauma

We categorized participants into four groups including no trauma exposure or one of three possible responses to trauma based on lifetime trauma exposure, probable lifetime PTSD, and psychological health (psychological distress and positive psychological well-being). Each psychological factor (as well as trauma exposure) was assessed at the 2008 substudy.

Lifetime trauma burden was assessed in the 2008 substudy via a modified version of the Brief Trauma Questionnaire (BTQ).62 The modified BTQ asked participants to report if they had experienced each of 15 different traumatic events in their lifetime and included an open-ended prompt assessing a “seriously traumatic event not already covered in any of these questions.” Among women who endorsed at least one traumatic event, their trauma burden was operationalized as the number of traumatic event types endorsed. See the eMethods (Supplemental Digital Content 2) for further details. Women who reported never experiencing a traumatic event were assigned to the “no trauma” group.

Probable lifetime PTSD as of 2008 was assessed via the Short Screening Scale for DSM-IV PTSD (SSS-IV).63 Women who experienced at least one traumatic event in their lifetime and reported ever experiencing four or more symptoms on the SSS-IV63 in their lifetime were categorized as having probable lifetime PTSD. Women who met criteria for probable lifetime PTSD were categorized in the “PTSD” group. In addition to reporting on lifetime PTSD symptoms, participants were asked to report their experience of the same set of PTSD symptoms in the preceding four weeks.

Coping without Thriving and Psychological Resilience were characterized according to lifetime trauma burden and a multidimensional measure of psychological health following prior work with this sample.51,64 First, we constructed a continuous score for psychological health by summing three z-scored measures of positive psychological well-being (happiness, hope, meaning in life) and reverse z-scored measures of psychological distress (i.e., depression symptoms, PTSD symptoms). Happiness and hope were measured via two positively worded items on the Center of Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, 10 item version (CES-D-10):65 “I felt hopeful about the future” and “I was happy” (Spearman’s correlation = 0.58). Meaning in life was evaluated via the following item from the Brief Multidimensional Measure of Religiousness and Spirituality, to which participants rated their agreement on a 4-point Likert scale: “I have a sense of mission or calling in my own life.”66 Depression symptoms were operationalized as the sum of the negatively worded items on the CES-D-10 (McDonald’s omega [ω] = 0.84), and PTSD symptoms were measured by the total score on the SSS-IV (ω = 0.84). Note that, although women who experienced probable lifetime PTSD were categorized separately, we included PTSD symptoms in the present measure because some women experienced subclinical symptoms of PTSD that may affect their psychological health.

We used this measure of psychological health in combination with information on trauma burden to characterize women as either “coping without thriving” or psychologically “resilient.” Specificually, we constructed a psychological resilience score by extracting the standardized residuals from regressing measured psychological health on lifetime trauma burden. This residual approach is an established strategy for operationalizing resilience as an outcome, quantifying the difference between an observed and predicted outcome.67

Coping without thriving was characterized by less favorable psychological health than expected given one’s trauma burden. Women were categorized as coping without thriving if they endorsed any lifetime trauma exposure and scored within the bottom two tertiles of the continuous psychological resilience score.

Psychological resilience was characterized by more favorable psychological health than expected given one’s trauma burden. Women were categorized as resilient if they scored within the upper tertile of the continuous psychological resilience measure. Additionally, to capture the full level of information available, we also derived a continuous measure characterizing psychological resilience to trauma and evaluated this in the context of trauma exposure and in relation to each outcome. This continuous measure of psychological resilience to trauma incorporates information on all elements of our categorization and reflects a continuum ranging from low (e.g., PTSD) to moderate (e.g., coping without thriving) to high (e.g., resilient) psychological health relative to one’s trauma burden without requiring a cut-point or assuming homogeneity within categories. Therefore, we also considered the association between continuous psychological resilience to trauma and probable MetS among women exposed to trauma within sensitivity analyses.

### Probable Metabolic Syndrome

MetS diagnosis is typically established when three of five criteria are met, including abdominal obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia.13 However, for the current study we could consider only four of the five criteria as hypertriglyceridemia was not assessed in the biennial questionnaires. We created a measure of probable metabolic syndrome (hereafter referred to as MetS) at each questionnaire year between 1989 and 2019 based on self-reported health information using four criteria (summarized in Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content 1): hyperlipidemia (clinician-diagnosed elevated cholesterol or use of cholesterol-lowering medications), hypertension (clinician-diagnosed hypertension or use of antihypertensive medications), diabetes (clinician-diagnosed diabetes or use of hypoglycemic medications), and overweight/obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥ 28 kg/m2 derived from self-reported height and weight). Note that the cut-off for the overweight/obesity criterion was selected based on evidence from the Nurses’ Health Study that BMI ≥ 28 kg/m2 corresponds to the same percentile for BMI as a waist circumference of 88 cm, the cut-off used in the diagnostic criteria for MetS.12 This approximation is consistent with prior research in a prospective cohort of men with the same study design as NHS2.68 Detailed information on how participants were asked about clinician-diagnosed medical conditions, which medications were assessed, and validation of self-reported health status information in NHS2 is available in the eMethods (Supplemental Digital Content 2). When participants first endorsed three of the four MetS criteria in questionnaire j, time to new onset MetS was approximated via the interval (agej-1, agej], where agej is age in months at the time of returning questionnaire j. We also investigated time to each MetS criterion to query if certain criteria were driving the association. The interval encompassing time to each MetS criterion was estimated similarly to overall MetS, but additional information on the timing of individual diagnoses were used when available to increase precision (see eMethods; Supplemental Digital Content 2).

Individuals were followed from their response to the 2009 biennial questionnaire until the first of development of probable MetS (or MetS criterion, for criterion-specific analyses), last responding questionnaire, or death. In all analyses, individuals were censored at age 70 to avoid sparse strata (<2500 person-months contributed after age 70 for all outcomes).

### Covariates

Covariates were selected based on prior literature suggesting they were related to response to trauma and MetS and could confound the associations of interest.69–71 Analyses adjusted for age; non-Hispanic White race/ethnicity; parental history of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, high blood pressure (HTN), or diabetes; maximum of parents’ educational achievement during childhood (high school or less, some college, college); BMI at age 18; and somatotype at age five. Parental educational attainment was included as a proxy for childhood socioeconomic status (SES), which has been associated with trauma exposure and long-term health.72–75 Somatotype at age five, intended as a proxy for childhood adiposity, was measured via a somatogram scale with nine pictograms. Participants selected the pictogram that best corresponded to their body size at age five, and responses were top coded at pictogram five.

Additional variables that could confound or mediate the response to trauma-MetS association were also considered in sensitivity analyses (all time-varying): cigarette smoking, physical activity, and diet (see eMethods for more information; Supplemental Digital Content 2). Cigarette smoking was assessed biennially from 1989 onwards. Physical activity was assessed in 1989 and every four years beginning in 1991. Diet was assessed every four years from 1989 onwards. Additionally, since antidepressant medications affect metabolism,76,77 we considered time-varying antidepressant use. Antidepressant use was ascertained via questions about regular use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs; biennially from 1997 onwards), tricyclic antidepressants (in 1997 and biennially from 2013 onwards), or other antidepressant medications (biennially from 2001 onwards) in the two years preceding a given questionnaire.

### Statistical Analyses

We first performed descriptive analyses of sociodemographic characteristics and plotted age-adjusted cumulative incidence curves for MetS and its components by trauma response type. Cumulative incidence curves were calculated as 1-S where S is the survival function estimated via the Kaplan-Meier estimator.78 Second, we evaluated variation in time to developing MetS by psychological resilience to trauma using interval-censored proportional hazards models, as implemented in the R statistical software (v4.3.2) package icenReg (v2.0.16), to account for interval censoring between questionnaire cycles.79 Specifically, rather than defining a specific event time as in traditional survival models, interval-censored models permit specification of an interval of time within which the event occurred. This approach produces hazard ratios but acknowledges uncertainty in event times within calculation of the log-likelihood via the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator, thereby producing more accurate standard error estimates and confidence intervals than would be obtained by assuming a specific event time.80 Standard errors and confidence intervals were calculated via cluster bootstrapping using 1000 bootstrapped samples.

We fit models in two steps. First, we examined associations with incident MetS with minimally adjusted models that included only age as a covariate. Second, we adjusted for potential confounders (i.e., non-Hispanic White race/ethnicity, childhood SES, and parental history of CVD, diabetes, or hypertension). Finally, separate minimally adjusted models and models adjusted for potential confounders were fit for each component of probable MetS excluding individuals with the outcome at baseline. We confirmed the proportional hazards assumption by visually comparing the log-log transformed baseline survival function estimated by semi-parametric survival models within each stratum of psychological response to trauma, adjusted for covariates.79

#### Sensitivity Analyses.

To evaluate if associations between psychological resilience to trauma and probable MetS could be confounded by social and behavioral factors related to health, analyses were repeated additionally including time-varying smoking, physical activity, and diet. We subsequently added time-varying antidepressant treatment in a second step. We recognize that some of these factors could additionally serve as mediators, but assessing mediation was outside the scope of the current work. Additionally, we repeated analyses among trauma-exposed women using the resilient group as the reference group to evaluate differences in the risk of MetS across resilient, coping without thriving, and PTSD groups. Then, to assess the consistency of our results when considering the full continuum of psychological health following trauma exposure, we evaluated the association between our continuous measure of psychological resilience to trauma and time to incident MetS among women exposed to trauma. Furthermore, since evaluating the association between the continuous resilience measure and MetS rate precluded comparisons to women with no trauma exposure, we also tested the associations of psychological health and trauma burden with the hazard of incident MetS. We included a product term between psychological well-being and trauma-burden to evaluate multiplicative effect measure modification (i.e., if the association between psychological well-being and the hazard of MetS varied with trauma burden). Additionally, to probe the association between MetS severity and psychological resilience to trauma, we used generalized estimating equations (GEEs) with a Poisson distribution and log link considering a count of MetS criteria endorsed at each questionnaire from 2009 to 2019. Relatedly, we considered associations of each specific component of psychological health with the hazard of incident MetS, to evaluate if the strength of associations might vary across components. Due to high correlations between components (range: −0.55 to 0.58; see Table S3), we considered five separate models with each component entered individually. Finally, to investigate if associations varied when considering current PTSD instead of lifetime PTSD, we repeated primary analyses categorizing only women who met criteria for PTSD in the preceding four weeks in the PTSD group (N = 492).

Overall, 6.4% of participants were missing data on at least one covariate, and 11.1% of observations were missing data on at least one covariate included in sensitivity analyses. Missingness in time invariant, categorical covariates was addressed via a missing category when over 100 individuals were missing a value, and via mode imputation when fewer than 100 values were missing.81 Missingness in time-varying covariates was addressed by carrying values forward up to four years where possible, and residual missingness was addressed via mean (for continuous covariates) or mode (for categorical covariates) imputation. All analyses were conducted in R Statistical Software (v4.3.2).82 This study did not employ a reporting guideline.

## Results

### Sample Characteristics

On average, participants were 54.3 (standard deviation [SD] = 4.6) years old in 2009 and 95.0% were non-Hispanic White (Table 1). 37,923 (89.4%) women endorsed at least one potentially traumatic experience. Among these, the most women were categorized as coping without thriving (N = 17,375 [41.0%]), followed by resilient (N = 11,871 [28.0%]), and then probable lifetime PTSD (N = 8,677 [20.5%]). Women who did not endorse any potentially traumatic events were categorized as having experienced no trauma (N = 4,502 [10.6%]).

Compared to the other groups, women who met criteria for PTSD were less likely to be married in 2009, more likely to endorse tobacco smoking as of 2009, more likely to report a parental history of stroke or myocardial infarction, and more likely to report regular use of antidepressants in 2009 than women characterized as coping without thriving, resilient, or trauma-unexposed (see Table 1). Descriptive statistics for the samples used in secondary analyses are available in Tables S4–S7 (Supplemental Digital Content 1).

### Associations with Incident Metabolic Syndrome

Over 2009 to 2019, 5,468 (12.9%) women developed MetS. Figure 1 presents the cumulative incidence curves for incident MetS from 2009 to 2019 by type of psychological response to trauma. Age-adjusted models demonstrate that women in the PTSD and coping without thriving groups consistently demonstrated a greater rate of incident probable MetS than women in the no trauma group.

Women with probable lifetime PTSD experienced a 34% greater hazard of developing MetS (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 1.34 [1.05, 1.71]) over the 10 years of follow-up relative to women with no trauma exposure, after adjusting for demographics, childhood adiposity, BMI at age 18, and parental history of cardiometabolic disease (see Figure 2). Similarly, women in the coping without thriving group experienced a 29% greater hazard of developing MetS (aHR = 1.29 [1.03, 1.62]) relative to the no trauma group after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and health history. In contrast, the hazard of developing MetS among women characterized as resilient was similar to that among women with no trauma exposure (aHR = 1.06 [0.84, 1.34]) after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and health history.

### Associations with Incident MetS Criteria

Age-adjusted cumulative incidence curves for MetS criteria by response to trauma are presented in Figures S2 and S3 (Supplemental Digital Content 1). Considering MetS components separately, although point estimates for all components were elevated for the PTSD and coping without thriving groups when compared to women with no history of trauma (Table S8, Supplemental Digital Content 1), only two reached statistical significance after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics and health history. Specifically, women with lifetime probable PTSD experienced a 40% greater hazard of developing diabetes (95% CI 1.06, 1.85) and a 47% greater hazard of becoming overweight/obese (95% CI 1.06, 2.05) relative to women with no trauma exposure, after adjusting for demographics and health history. In contrast, women who were classified as resilient experienced a similar hazard of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and overweight as the no trauma group across follow-up (see Figure 2). Although the coefficients estimating the relative hazards of developing hypertension and hyperlipidemia among the women classified as coping without thriving or with probable PTSD were elevated after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics and health history, they did not reach statistical significance in either crude analyses or those adjusted for potential confounders (see Table S8, Supplemental Digital Content 1).

### Sensitivity Analyses

Models adjusting for all potential confounders as well as smoking, diet, and physical activity (see Figure 2) and then further adding antidepressant use (see Table S8, Supplemental Digital Content 1) produced similar results to those in our primary analyses. Analyses restricted to women exposed to trauma confirmed that women categorized as coping without thriving (HR = 1.22 [1.06, 1.40]) or PTSD (HR = 1.26 [1.08, 1.48]) experienced an elevated rate of MetS over 10 years of follow-up relative to women categorized as resilient. Consistent with these findings, among women exposed to trauma, a one standard deviation increase in the continuous psychological resilience score was associated with a 14% reduction in the hazard of developing MetS over follow-up (HR = 0.86 [0.81, 0.91]) after adjusting for potential confounders. Results were unchanged after further adjusting for trauma burden. Estimates attenuated with adjustment for health behaviors and antidepressant use but remained statistically significant (see Table S9, Supplemental Digital Content 1). Similarly, when including women with no trauma history, a one standard deviation (SD) increase in psychological health was associated with a 16.6% reduction in the hazard of MetS (95% CI 0.74, 0.94) after adjusting for potential confounders. There was no evidence for an independent association between trauma burden and the hazard of MetS (HR = 1.02 [0.99, 1.04]), nor for a multiplicative interaction between psychological well-being and trauma burden (HR = 1.01 [0.99, 1.03]). After adjustment for health behaviors and antidepressant use, the coefficient for psychological health attenuated and was no longer statistically significant (HR = 0.89 [0.79, 1.01]), whereas the coefficient for trauma burden was marginally statistically significant (HR = 1.03 [1.00, 1.06]; see Table S9, Supplemental Digital Content 1).

After adjusting for demographic characteristics, BMI at age 18, childhood adiposity, and childhood SES, women in the coping without thriving and PTSD groups met 9% (95% CI 1.06, 1.12) and 11% (95% CI 1.08, 1.14) more MetS criteria than the no trauma group over follow-up, respectively. The number of prevalent MetS criteria met over follow-up did not differ between resilient and trauma unexposed women (ratio of expected counts = 1.01 [0.98, 1.04]). However, after adjustment for health behaviors and antidepressant use, resilient women met 4% (95% CI 1.01, 1.06) more prevalent MetS criteria than the no trauma group over follow-up. Estimates for women in the coping without thriving and PTSD groups remained similar after further adjustment (see Table S10, Supplemental Digital Content 1).

In models investigating associations of individual components of the psychological health measure with incident MetS among women exposed to trauma, a one standard deviation (SD) increase in current PTSD or depressive symptoms was associated with an elevated hazard, whereas a one SD increase in happiness or hopefulness was associated with lower hazards of incident MetS (Table S11, Supplemental Digital Content 1). Finally, in analyses of past-month PTSD relative to no trauma, 72.4% (N = 6,284) of the women in the lifetime PTSD group moved into the coping without thriving group and 21.9% (N = 1,904) moved into the resilient group. Point-estimates adjusted for potential confounders show trends suggesting that past-month PTSD may be more strongly associated with time to incident MetS than lifetime PTSD (HRcurrent PTSD = 1.69 [1.02, 2.80] versus HRlifetime PTSD = 1.34 [1.05, 1.71]). However, the results of this sensitivity analysis should be interpreted with caution due to small cell sizes (PTSD: N = 492; Tabel S12, Supplemental Digital Content 1).

## Discussion

In the present investigation, we found that trauma exposure accompanied by high positive psychological well-being and low psychological distress (e.g. psychological resilience) was not associated with an increased rate of incident MetS relative to women with no trauma exposure. In contrast, psychological responses to trauma characterized by psychological distress and/or low levels of positive psychological well-being (PTSD and coping without thriving) were associated with an elevated rate of developing MetS relative to not experiencing trauma or to maintaining high psychological well-being following trauma exposure (resilient). Together, these results suggest that it is unresolved psychological distress following trauma exposure (a combination of higher psychological distress and/or lower positive psychological well-being) and not trauma itself that may confer increased risk of metabolic disruptions. This conclusion is further supported by the lack of evidence for an association between trauma burden and risk for MetS after adjusting for psychological well-being. Such findings suggest that disrupting the harmful effects of trauma exposure on psychological health may benefit not only psychological functioning but also have downstream benefits for physical health as well.

Existing research using similar outcome-based measures of psychological resilience have found that higher resilience was prospectively associated with lower risk of cardiometabolic outcomes and all-cause mortality over six years.44 Our findings are also congruent with other prior work assessing psychological well-being which suggests that higher versus lower psychological well-being is similarly associated with lower risk of developing CVD,83 mortality due to CVD,84 and metabolic syndrome components,49 including dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hypertriglyceridemia.85 For example, in an analysis of 3,254 adults in the Midlife in the United States Study prospective cohort, among individuals exposed to early-life adversity, those who demonstrated low psychological well-being experienced 43% greater odds of cardiometabolic conditions than those with high positive psychological well-being (who could be considered as demonstrating psychological resilience).50 Our findings are also consistent with literature suggesting that higher levels of psychological distress and lower psychological well-being are associated with more physical health problems generally86 and greater risk of having or developing MetS specifically.20 Moreover, there is evidence that PTSD symptom remission is associated with fewer cardiovascular events,87 reduced risk of type 2 diabetes,88 and fewer complications of type 2 diabetes.89 Consistent with a decline in risk for cardiometabolic complications with PTSD symptom remission, we found suggestive evidence that current PTSD may be more strongly associated with risk of incident MetS than lifetime PTSD, although confidence intervals were wide and overlapping. This body of evidence together with the results presented here supports the interpretation that psychological resilience may buffer against the negative health effects commonly associated with trauma exposure.

Relatedly, our finding that subclinical levels of psychological distress in combination with lower levels of positive psychological well-being are associated with an increased risk of MetS is consistent with previous research on depression trajectories and health.90,91 In an analysis of over 19,000 community-dwelling older adults, individuals with persistent subclinical depressive symptoms over five years experienced increased risk for diabetes, obesity, abdominal obesity, and MetS relative to nondepressed individuals. The magnitude of this increase was smaller than that observed among individuals with persistent clinical depression but nevertheless statistically significant.91 Similarly, in both analyses considering lifetime and current PTSD, the point estimates for the association between PTSD and incident MetS were higher than that for coping without thriving (subclinical psychological distress/low positive psychological well-being). Together, evidence from the present analysis and extant literature suggests that even subclinical psychological distress may confer increased risk for MetS. Although outside the scope of the current work, future research may benefit from considering the association between MetS and general psychological distress after trauma92 in addition to investigating specific manifestations of distress such as PTSD.

In the present analysis, out of the three facets of positive psychological well-being investigated, higher past-week happiness and hopefulness were associated with a lower risk of incident MetS independent of other covariates, with a weaker and statistically non-significant association evident for sense of meaning in life. These findings align with extant literature, which supports an association between each and cardiometabolic health with reasonable consistency.93 Notably, all positive components were measured using single questions and thus were limited in their ability to individually measure variability in participants’ experiences of positive psychological well-being.94 Future research leveraging more comprehensive measures and accounting for the shared variance between them will be necessary to disentangle the contributions of different aspects of psychological health to risk for MetS following trauma exposure.

One plausible mechanism by which psychological distress and lower levels of positive psychological well-being could influence risk for MetS is via health behaviors. Trauma exposure, PTSD, and depression have been associated with increased engagement in behavioral risk factors for MetS, including tobacco smoking,95–97 unhealthy diet,98,99 and reduced physical activity.100–102 Other studies have found psychological resilience to stress is inversely associated with the same risk factors.52,103 Therefore, resilient women may not experience an elevated risk of MetS because they are less likely to engage in health risk behaviors, whereas women who experience psychological distress may be at elevated risk at least in part, because they are more likely to engage in such behaviors.

Another potential explanation lies in the higher proportion of women taking antidepressant medications in the coping without thriving and PTSD groups relative to both the resilient and trauma unexposed groups. Antidepressant medications are known to carry risk for weight gain and development of metabolic abnormalities,104,105 and have been associated with increased odds of MetS independent of depressive symptoms.106 Notably, although the present study did not evaluate mediation, the estimated association between trauma response and probable MetS persisted after adjusting for smoking, unhealthy diet, physical activity, and antidepressant use, suggesting that these potential mechanisms cannot fully explain the observed associations.

### Strengths and Limitations

Confidence in our findings is supported by our use of a large, well-characterized longitudinal cohort and prospective study design. In addition, our investigation of trauma response and MetS in a sample of civilian women expands the existing literature on MetS, which primarily used samples of military men.20 Another strength of our study is our transdiagnostic and strengths-based conceptualization of resilience, which accounts not only for the absence of PTSD or psychological distress but also for the presence of elements of positive psychological well-being. Moreover, our operationalization of resilience accounted for variation in trauma burden, acknowledging that resilience may look different in the context of numerous versus few traumatic experience types.

Data limitations necessitated using self-report measures to approximate MetS, hyperlipidemia in place of dyslipidemia, a proxy measure of abdominal obesity, and precluded accounting for hypertriglyceridemia. However, validation studies within NHS2 indicate high concordance between objective measures and self-reported height, weight,107 diabetes,108 and hypertension.109 Moreover, the study population of nurses was selected in part because they are more likely to report health data accurately.60 Nevertheless, future research among samples with empirical measures of MetS criteria is necessary to confirm these findings. In addition, the present analysis necessarily excluded women who had developed MetS prior to measurement of trauma exposure when participants were, on average, 54 years-old. Although risk for metabolic syndrome increases with age, it is commonly diagnosed in early and middle adulthood110,111 or even adolescence.112 Consequently, this sample may be healthier than the general population at risk for MetS. To the extent that the individuals most susceptible to developing MetS were excluded for prevalent disease, the present analysis may underestimate the true association between psychological resilience to trauma and incident MetS. Our study is also limited by its relatively homogeneous sample, which consists primarily of White-identified, educated women. Finally, as an observational study, our analysis is inherently vulnerable to potential unmeasured confounding and thus cannot make causal claims about the association between psychological responses to trauma and MetS.

### Implications for Research and Practice

Our findings have important implications for clinical practice and future research. First, they suggest the value of considering increased screening for MetS among women with a history of trauma exposure and psychological distress. Identification of early-stage disease is key to preventing or slowing disease progression and the development of comorbidities, but guidelines for early intervention in cardiometabolic health do not address the increased risk associated with psychiatric disorders and psychological distress more generally.113,114 Relatedly, mental health clinicians should be aware of and provide psychoeducation about the potential physical health risks associated with trauma-related distress, particularly in older adult women. Therapeutic strategies that bolster resilience to trauma rather than focusing only on symptom reduction may further protect physical health and improve mental health following trauma exposure. Additionally, since antidepressant medications are known to differ in their metabolic effects,104 selection of a treatment regimen to address psychological disorders should include careful consideration of the patient’s risk for cardiometabolic conditions.

Similarly, since psychological resilience may serve as a modifiable protective factor against the development of MetS, screening for trauma exposure and positive psychological well-being, as well as distress among women who are at elevated risk of developing MetS may be useful to identify potential prevention targets. Meta-analyses of interventions to promote psychological resilience suggest that resilience is modifiable and that increasing psychological resilience is associated with reduced distress.115,116 Limited evidence suggests that interventions to improve psychological well-being are associated with a reduction in risk factors for cardiovascular health at both biological117,118 and behavioral119,120 levels. A meta-analysis of 19 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found that stress reduction interventions, largely comprising cognitive behavioral therapy or mindfulness training, were associated with clinically significant reductions in C-reactive protein levels, which is robustly associated with cardiovascular risk.121,122 These results support the efficacy of targeting psychosocial factors for the treatment and prevention of cardiometabolic disorders.

Similarly, evidence from randomized controlled trials supports the efficacy of psychosocial interventions in treating metabolic syndrome and its criteria.123–126 A meta-analysis of 25 RCTs evaluating stress management interventions in the treatment of MetS found statistically significant reductions in fasting blood sugar, 2-hour postprandial blood sugar, weight, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol but not serum triglyceride levels.125 Additionally, a meta-analysis of 182 studies investigating the efficacy of stress reduction interventions to reduce blood pressure among individuals with hypertension found that a variety of interventions resulted in moderate decreases in systolic and diastolic blood pressure for up to three months.127

Future research is necessary to evaluate whether interventions to promote psychological resilience to trauma can reduce risk for metabolic syndrome and engagement in health risk behaviors (i.e., smoking, unhealthy diet, sedentary lifestyle). In addition, studies aiming to elucidate the mechanisms underlying linkages between trauma exposure and adverse physical health outcomes should look beyond binary exposures (such as PTSD vs. no PTSD) to acknowledge the substantial heterogeneity in responses to trauma and the resulting variation in patterns of risk for adverse sequelae. Furthermore, in line with accumulating evidence for the protective effects of positive health factors,46,128 such work should include consideration of positive elements of psychological well-being rather than investigating psychopathology in isolation.

### Conclusion

In a large cohort of older women, risk for developing MetS was similar across women who were psychologically resilient to trauma (reporting high positive psychological well-being relative to their trauma burden) and women with no trauma history. In contrast, increased risk of MetS was associated with being trauma exposed and experiencing severe psychological distress (e.g. PTSD). Perhaps more surprisingly, higher risk was also evident among trauma-exposed women who did not necessarily report high levels of distress but reported low levels of psychological well-being, what some investigators have previously termed ‘malaise’.129,130 Overall, these findings underscore the potential protective role of positive psychological well-being and resilience in mitigating risk for MetS among trauma-exposed women. Interventions aimed at promoting psychological well-being in addition to reducing distress may present promising approaches for reducing not only the significant burden of trauma among women, but also downstream effects on their physical health.
